primary.rationale: The talk is about writing, structuring, and maintaining agent skill.md files that program LLM behavior through natural-language instructions, leading words, and deletion testing. The framework targets developers building AI agent skills across general-purpose applications rather than a specific vertical. The checklist covers designing skills (trigger, structure), building them (steering with leading words and splitting), and maintaining them (pruning sediment and no-ops). Requires familiarity with AI agent skill systems and context windows but is accessible to practicing developers. Delivered as a structured conference-style talk with slides, code demonstrations, and a downloadable skill artifact. summary: Matt Pocock frames the current landscape of AI agent skills as "skill hell," analogous to earlier tutorial hell and framework hell, where abundance without quality criteria leaves developers and organizations unable to evaluate or improve skills effectively. He attributes this to the absence of a shared rubric and introduces a four-part checklist: Trigger, Structure, Steering, and Pruning. On Trigger, he distinguishes user-invoked from model-invoked skills. Model-invoked skills place a description (context pointer) in the agent's context at all times, letting the agent decide when to load the full skill.md, while user-invoked skills hide this description, requiring manual invocation. Model-invoked skills offer flexibility but increase context load and unpredictability; user-invoked skills reduce agent context load and remove a class of unpredictability but shift cognitive burden to the pilot. On Structure, he identifies two core units: steps (procedures) and reference (supporting information). He advocates minimizing skill.md for maintainability, auditability, and token cost. Branch-specific reference material should be moved behind context pointers—external references in separate markdown files bundled with the skill—that the agent pulls in only when needed. On Steering, he introduces "leading words," dense phrases that pack meaning into a small space. When placed in skill text, agents repeat these words in reasoning traces, reinforcing desired behavior. The "vertical slice" example shows how a well-known term triggers the agent's priors to prevent layer-by-layer coding. He also addresses insufficient legwork by splitting skills into separate skills—like separating "grill with docs" (clarifying questions) from 2PRD (planning)—so the agent only sees one step at a time and invests more effort in each. On Pruning, he warns against duplication (maintain a single source of truth), sediment (irrelevant legacy material from collaborative editing), and no-ops (instructions that don't change agent behavior, detectable via deletion tests). He recommends running the "writing great skills" skill from his repo to evaluate and improve skills, and points to his newsletter at aihero.dev and an upcoming AI coding crash course.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.

takeaways: Skill hell stems from having many skills available without a shared rubric to evaluate or improve them.
The checklist framework has four parts: Trigger, Structure, Steering, and Pruning.
Model-invoked skills increase context load and unpredictability; user-invoked skills increase cognitive load on the pilot.
Skills should be organized into steps (procedures) and reference (supporting information), with branch-specific reference moved behind context pointers to external files.
Leading words—dense, reusable phrases—guide agent behavior by appearing in reasoning traces and triggering the agent's priors.
Splitting skills into separate skills hides future steps and increases per-step legwork when the agent doesn't do enough work on a particular phase.
Pruning removes duplication (single source of truth), sediment (irrelevant legacy material), and no-ops (instructions that don't change behavior, found via deletion tests).
Keeping skill.md minimal reduces maintenance burden, audit complexity, and per-request token cost.

sections.title: Introduction and Skill Hell
sections.summary: Matt introduces 'skill hell' as the current state where developers and organizations have access to many skills but cannot distinguish good from bad or understand how pieces fit together, paralleling earlier tutorial hell and framework hell. He identifies the missing piece as a shared rubric for evaluating skills.

sections.title: Overview of the Skill Checklist Framework
sections.summary: Introduces the four-part checklist: Trigger (how skill is invoked), Structure (internal layout), Steering (guiding agent behavior), and Pruning (minimizing the skill). Mentions the 'writing great skills' skill in his repo as an encoded version of this checklist.

sections.title: Trigger: User-Invoked vs Model-Invoked Skills
sections.summary: Compares user-invoked and model-invoked skills. Model-invoked skills place a description in agent context as a context pointer, increasing context load and unpredictability. User-invoked skills hide the description, reducing agent context load but increasing pilot cognitive load. Contrasts Matt Pocock skills (user-invoked, control-focused) with Superpowers (model-invoked, flexibility-focused).

sections.title: Structure: Steps and Reference
sections.summary: Identifies two core units for skills: steps (procedures) and reference (supporting information). Demonstrates with the 2PRD skill, which has three steps and two reference items on a single branch.

sections.title: Making the Skill.md File Minimal
sections.summary: Advocates minimizing skill.md for maintainability, auditability, and token cost. Branch-specific reference material should be moved behind context pointers to external markdown files bundled with the skill, which the agent pulls in only when needed. Uses domain modeling skill as an example of branching where ADR and context.md templates are only needed on specific branches.

sections.title: Steering: Leading Words
sections.summary: Introduces leading words—dense phrases that pack meaning into a small space. When placed in skill text, agents repeat these words in reasoning traces, reinforcing desired behavior. The 'vertical slice' example shows how a well-known term triggers the agent's priors to prevent layer-by-layer coding. Consistency and watching reasoning traces confirms effectiveness.

sections.title: Increasing Legwork Per Step
sections.summary: Addresses insufficient agent effort on specific steps like clarifying questions in plan mode. Solution: split skills into separate skills so the agent only sees one step at a time, hiding future goals. Example: grill with docs (clarifying questions) as a separate skill followed by 2PRD (planning) as another, increasing focus and effort per phase.

sections.title: Pruning: Duplication, Sediment, and No-ops
sections.summary: Identifies failure modes that bloat skills: duplication (maintain a single source of truth across steps and reference), sediment (irrelevant legacy material from collaborative editing that should be restructured or killed), and no-ops (instructions that appear to do something but don't change agent behavior, detectable via deletion tests).

sections.title: Final Summary and Resources
sections.summary: Recaps the full checklist: check trigger firing and context vs cognitive load, structure into steps and reference with branch material behind context pointers, steer with leading words and legwork management, and prune for sediment, crud, and no-ops. Points to the 'writing great skills' skill in his repo, his newsletter at aihero.dev, and an upcoming AI coding crash course.

demonstrations: 2PRD skill: three steps (find relevant context, confirm test seams with user, write PRD) with two reference items, all on a single branch.
Grill me skill: uses 'disable model invocation true' to make it user-invoked only.
Code base design skill: shown as a model-invocable skill with a description in agent context.
Domain modeling skill: has two or three branches (update glossary, create ADRs, or neither), making branch-specific templates candidates for removal from main skill.md.
Vertical slice: leading word used to prevent layer-by-layer coding by triggering the agent's priors about slicing work vertically.
Grill with docs: split from plan mode into a separate skill for clarifying questions, followed by 2PRD as a separate skill, so the agent only sees one step at a time.
No-op example: a paragraph in an implement skill instructing the agent to write a detailed commit message, which the agent would likely do anyway if the paragraph were deleted.
limitations: Model-invoked skills require evaluation to ensure they are called at the right time.
User-invoked skills require the pilot to deeply understand available skills to use them effectively.
Organizations lack understanding of how to convert operating procedures into effective agent skills.
Splitting skills to increase legwork is not always necessary; use selectively for specific high-effort phases.
quantitativeClaims: A hundred model-invoked skills means a hundred descriptions inside the agent's context.
Every word shaved from a skill.md file saves multiple tokens per request.
